title: 'You are like me'
short: Gilgamish is surprised that the immortal Flood hero looks just like him and lies idly on his back.
body: The disappointment sets the tone of Tablet XI: immortality came to Uta-Napishtim as a unique gift of the gods, not by heroic achievement. Gilgamish had prepared to fight him. The question 'how did you stand in the assembly of the gods and find life?' introduces the Flood story as an answer. George translates the opening similarly, with Gilgamish's 'heart' having imagined him as a warrior.

A. R. George, The Epic of Gilgamesh: A New Translation (London: Penguin, 1999), Tablet XI

title: The secret of the gods
short: Uta-Napishtim reveals 'a hidden matter, a secret of the gods': the Flood story is presented as esoteric knowledge.
body: The phrase recalls the prologue (I), where Gilgamish 'discovered the secret concealed' and brought back knowledge from before the Flood. The poem thus closes its circle: the reader now hears that secret. The same phrasing is used again for the plant of rejuvenation ('a hidden matter'), so Gilgamish is twice given secret knowledge in this tablet. Thompson's 'rede of the Gods' renders the 'secret' in archaic English.

title: Shuruppak
short: Shuruppak, modern Fara, is the Flood hero's city on the Euphrates.
body: Thompson's note: 'The modern Fara.' Excavations there have revealed a flood layer, though scholars caution against linking any single local flood to the myth. In the Sumerian King List Shuruppak is the last city with kingship before the Flood, under Ubar-Tutu. Its age ('Old is this city, with gods in its midst') roots the story in sacred history. Shuruppak is also the city of the wise Shuruppak in Sumerian wisdom literature.

title: The Flood and its sources
short: The gods decide to send a Flood: the story is adapted from the older Atrahasis epic and closely parallels Genesis 6-9.
body: Tigay showed that Tablet XI was taken over from the Old Babylonian Atrahasis epic, sometimes almost word for word, and inserted into the late version. In Atrahasis the gods send the Flood because the noise of over-multiplying humanity disturbs Enlil's sleep; Tablet XI gives no reason at all, which makes the gods' decision seem arbitrary. Genesis gives a moral reason: the wickedness of man (Genesis 6:5). The parallels with Genesis (divine warning, ark, pitch, animals, mountain, birds, sacrifice, divine smelling of the savour, promise) were first announced by George Smith in 1872 and remain the best-known link between Mesopotamian and Biblical literature.

title: The gods of the Flood council
short: Anu their father, Enlil their counsellor, Ninurta their chamberlain, Ennugi their canal-inspector: the gods decide on the Flood.
body: Thompson gives Ninurta as 'herald' and Ennugi as 'leader(?)'. Modern translations call Ennugi the canal-controller (gugallu), an irrigation official: the gods are listed like officials of a Babylonian administration. The same list occurs in Atrahasis. Ea is present but bound by oath. Listing the gods by their administrative offices is a touch of irony at the expense of the divine bureaucracy that decides to destroy mankind, and it shows the Gilgamesh poet following his source closely. Anu presides, Enlil plans, and lesser gods execute.

title: Nin-igi-azag (Ea)
short: Nin-igi-azag, 'Lord of the clear eye', is a title of Ea, god of wisdom.
body: The name emphasises Ea's cleverness. Bound by oath not to reveal the gods' plan to a human, he gets round it by speaking to a wall. Thompson keeps the Sumerian epithet and identifies it in the line: ''tis Ea'. Ea was also called Nudimmud and Enki. His characteristic intelligence (he is the god of wisdom, incantations and crafts) is exactly what is needed to save mankind against Enlil's will. His trick of speaking to a wall preserves his oath while revealing the secret, a legalistic solution that the poem clearly enjoys.

sources.cite: R. Campbell Thompson, The Epic of Gilgamish: A New Translation (London: Luzac, 1928), Eleventh Tablet, Ea

Stephanie Dalley, Myths from Mesopotamia: Creation, the Flood, Gilgamesh, and Others (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1989; rev. 2000), glossary, s.v. Ea

title: Ea speaks to the reed wall
short: Ea, sworn to secrecy, tells the plan to a reed wall so that the man behind it overhears: a legal trick.
body: By speaking to the wall Ea can claim he never told a human; later he tells Enlil that he only sent the Flood hero a dream. The reed hut was the typical dwelling of the marshes. The same device occurs in Atrahasis. Ea's command, 'abandon wealth, seek life', is the ethical centre of the story. Thompson's repeated 'O Reed-hut, O Reed-hut! Wall, wall!' preserves the incantatory effect of the original.

title: 'Pull down your house, build a boat'
short: Ea commands: pull down the house, build a boat, abandon possessions, save life, take aboard the seed of all living things.
body: Compare Genesis 6:14-21, where God orders Noah to make an ark and bring in the animals. The phrase 'seek life' resonates with Gilgamish's own quest. The reed house becomes the boat, as reed was the material of southern boats. The command reverses the normal values of a householder: destroy your house, abandon your property, save only life. The repeated words for 'life' (napistu) echo in the hero's name, Uta-napishti, 'he found life'. Gilgamish, who is seeking life, is thus told the story of a man who found it by obeying a god.

sources.cite: R. Campbell Thompson, The Epic of Gilgamish: A New Translation (London: Luzac, 1928), Eleventh Tablet, Ea's speech

title: Ea's deceptive message
short: Ea tells Uta-Napishtim to tell the people that Enlil will rain down abundance: puns that also mean disaster.
body: Thompson calls the lines 'difficult'. Commentators, George among them, explain the wordplay: kukku 'cakes' and kibati 'wheat' sound like Akkadian words of ill omen (for darkness and for heaviness or misfortune). The people hear a promise; the gods mean destruction. Dalley and George both discuss the ambiguity. Ea's instructions show that the Flood hero must deceive his own city, which raises moral questions that the text does not address. Thompson's note simply marks the lines as difficult.

title: The ark: a cube
short: The boat is ten gar high and ten across, with seven decks and nine compartments: a perfect cube.
body: Genesis 6:15 gives the ark as 300 cubits long, 50 wide and 30 high, a rectangular box; the Babylonian vessel is a cube of about 60 metres on each side, divided into seven decks and nine compartments. Some scholars have suggested the cube is symbolic, perhaps modelled on a temple or the cosmos; others note that it would not float well as a boat. In Atrahasis the boat is described differently again.

title: Bitumen, pitch and the shar
short: The hull is coated with bitumen and pitch measured in shar, a unit of 3,600: enormous quantities.
body: Thompson leaves 'shar' (sar) untranslated; as a number it means 3,600, so 'six shar' implies a vast amount (Thompson's note gives the variant 'three'). Bitumen from natural seepages was used in Mesopotamia to waterproof boats and baskets. Genesis 6:14 likewise has Noah 'pitch it within and without with pitch'. The same word shar appears with a different value (an area) in the description of Uruk at the end of this tablet.

The Bible, Authorized (King James) Version, Genesis 6:14

title: A feast like the New Year
short: The workmen drink beer and wine like river water and feast as on the New Year festival.
body: The New Year (akitu) festival was the greatest celebration of the Babylonian calendar, held in spring at Babylon with processions, feasting and the recitation of the creation epic. Thompson's note: 'lit. water of the river'. The joyous feast of the builders contrasts darkly with the destruction to come, of which they know nothing. The detail adds to the epic's realism.

title: 'The seed of all living things'
short: Uta-Napishtim loads silver, gold, his family, craftsmen and 'the seed of all living things' into the ark.
body: Compare Genesis 6:19-20 and 7:2-3, where Noah takes pairs (or sevens) of every animal. The Babylonian hero also takes craftsmen, so that civilisation, not only life, survives the Flood. The inclusion of silver and gold contradicts Ea's command to abandon wealth, a detail critics have noticed. The phrase 'seed of all living things' is close to the Biblical idiom of keeping 'seed alive upon the face of all the earth' (Genesis 7:3).

title: Adad, the storm-god
short: Adad, god of storm and rain, thunders inside the black cloud that rises from the horizon.
body: Adad (Hadad in Syria) controlled rain and thunder; his symbol was the lightning fork. In Atrahasis he is also the god who withholds rain to cause famine. Here he brings the Flood's darkness that 'turned to blackness all that was light'. The storm arrives at dawn, as Shamash had appointed, and rises from the horizon as a black cloud, with Adad thundering inside it. The storm-god's role makes the Flood a meteorological catastrophe as well as a mythical one: rain, wind and darkness.

title: Nabu and Sharru: Shullat and Hanish
short: Thompson's 'Nabu and Sharru' are read by modern editors as Shullat and Hanish, two storm-gods who go before Adad.
body: The signs can be read in different ways; George reads Shullat and Hanish, divine heralds of the storm-god, known from other texts as a pair. Nabu, the scribe-god of Borsippa, would be out of place here. The storm is presented as an army on the march, with heralds, a vanguard and torch-bearers (the Anunnaki), led by Adad the storm-god. Thompson's reading reflects older scholarship.

title: Irragal (Errakal) and Ninurta
short: Irragal, a form of Nergal, tears out the mooring posts (Thompson's 'bollards') and Ninurta makes the dykes overflow.
body: Errakal is a name of Nergal, the god of plague and the underworld. Tearing out the mooring posts may refer to the posts of the cosmic waters or to the dams; George translates 'Errakal was uprooting the mooring poles'. Ninurta, Thompson's 'Havoc ... let loose', in modern editions makes the weirs overflow. The picture of the gods tearing down the cosmic structures shows that the Flood is a reversal of creation, a return to the waters of chaos.

title: The gods cower like dogs
short: Terrified by their own Flood, the gods flee to Anu's heaven and cower 'like curs' against the wall.
body: The simile is daring: the gods, who decreed the destruction, are reduced to frightened animals. It belongs to the epic's critical view of the divine council. In Atrahasis the gods also suffer, going hungry and thirsty without human offerings, which explains why they later 'gather like flies' over the sacrifice. Thompson's 'curs' is a vivid choice for kalbu, 'dog', and keeps the contempt of the image.

anchor: like to a woman in travail
title: Ishtar cries like a woman in childbirth
short: Ishtar, 'the sweet-voiced Lady of the gods', cries out like a woman in labour, regretting that she agreed to the destruction of her people.
body: The text calls her Ishtar, but the 'Lady of the gods' (Belet-ili) is the mother-goddess who created mankind, and in Atrahasis the lament belongs to the mother-goddess Nintu. The Gilgamesh poet has identified the two. The image of birth fits her role as creatrix: she gave birth to people only to see them float like fish-spawn. Thompson renders her title 'the sweet-spoken Lady'.

title: 'Like fish-spawn'
short: The drowned bodies fill the sea like the spawn of fish: one of the starkest images of the Flood.
body: The goddess laments that she gave birth to her people only for them to fill the sea. The image appears in Atrahasis too, where the dead clog the river like dragonflies; compare the kulilu-image of Tablet X. Such images express divine regret, a theme shared with Genesis 6:6 ('it repented the LORD that he had made man'). Thompson's rendering keeps the grim image.

title: Six days and seven nights of storm
short: The storm lasts six days and seven nights; on the seventh day it stops. In Genesis the rain lasts forty days.
body: Genesis 7:12 has forty days and nights of rain, and the waters prevail 150 days (7:24). The Babylonian timescale is much shorter, using the poem's formula of completion. The image of the storm 'fighting like an army' gives way to silence: 'all mankind had returned to clay', recalling the clay of creation (Aruru, Tablet I). The seventh day brings calm, as in the creation week.

title: Mount Nisir (Nimush)
short: The ark grounds on Mount Nisir, as older scholars read the name; George reads Nimush. In Genesis the ark rests 'upon the mountains of Ararat'.
body: The reading 'Nisir' was standard in Thompson's day; the signs are now read Nimush (George 2003). The mountain is usually located in the Zagros, east of the Tigris; an Assyrian royal inscription mentions it. Genesis 8:4 has the ark come to rest on the mountains of Ararat (Urartu), in Armenia. The day-by-day count ('one day, two days...') is a typical repetition of the epic.

title: The dove, the swallow and the raven
short: Uta-Napishtim sends out a dove and a swallow, which return, and then a raven, which does not: a close parallel to Genesis 8.
body: In Genesis 8:6-12 Noah sends a raven, which goes back and forth, then a dove three times; the second returns with an olive leaf, the third does not return. The Babylonian order differs, but the narrative logic (a bird that does not return shows dry land) is identical. This is one of the most striking details showing a literary relationship between the traditions; Tigay and Lambert discuss whether it is direct or mediated.

title: The gods gather like flies
short: The gods smell the sweet savour of the sacrifice and gather like flies: Genesis 8:21 says the LORD 'smelled a sweet savour'.
body: After days without offerings the hungry gods swarm over the sacrifice. The simile is satirical, though it also reflects the theology that the gods depend on human worship (explicit in Atrahasis). Genesis 8:20-21 keeps the sacrifice and the smell but removes the irony. Thompson's 'twice seven flagons' correspond to the 'seven and seven' cult vessels of modern translations, with reed, cedar and myrtle heaped beneath.

title: The mother-goddess's necklace
short: The goddess swears by her necklace, made by Anu, never to forget these days; modern editions read beads of lapis lazuli shaped as flies.
body: Thompson's 'necklet of sapphires' renders lapis lazuli (uqnu). George reads 'the great flies' that Anu made for her: fly-shaped beads, which pick up the simile of the gods gathering 'like flies'. In Atrahasis the mother-goddess likewise swears by her fly-necklace. Some have compared the rainbow as a sign of remembrance in Genesis 9:13-16, though the analogy is loose. The image of remembrance is powerful.

title: The Igigi
short: The Igigi are the great gods of heaven, often contrasted with the Anunnaki of the underworld.
body: Thompson's note: 'Gods of heaven.' In Atrahasis the Igigi are the junior gods who first did the labour of digging canals and rebelled, leading to the creation of humans. Enlil's fury at finding a survivor is directed against them as a group, since he suspects betrayal. In this passage the distinction is loose. The two groups, Igigi and Anunnaki, together make up the whole divine population.

anchor: visit his sin on the sinner
title: 'Lay his sin on the sinner'
short: Ea rebukes Enlil: punish the guilty, but do not destroy all; send a lion, a wolf, famine or plague instead of a Flood.
body: Ea's speech is a striking statement of individual justice: collective punishment is wrong. Compare Ezekiel 18:20, 'the soul that sinneth, it shall die', and Abraham's question in Genesis 18:25. The alternatives (lion, wolf, famine, plague) are the ordinary disasters that limit human numbers, as in Atrahasis. The speech, unusually, criticises the chief executive of the gods openly, and it persuades him: Enlil then blesses the survivors.

title: Alternatives to the Flood
short: Lion, wolf (Thompson 'jackal'), famine and the plague-god Erra: the four lesser scourges Ea proposes.
body: George reads the second beast as a wolf. The 'Plague-god' is Erra, the god of pestilence. These punishments are ordinary features of life; the point is that limited evils are preferable to annihilation. Compare the four 'sore judgments' of Ezekiel 14:21: sword, famine, noisome beast and pestilence. Thompson's 'jackal' was a common rendering in his time, as in the Shepherd episode of Tablet VI.

title: Atrahasis, 'Exceedingly Wise'
short: Ea says he only sent a dream to 'the Exceedingly Wise' (Atrahasis), the name of the Flood hero in the older epic.
body: Thompson's note identifies the title with Atra-hasis, another name for Uta-Napishtim. The slip of name betrays the source: the Old Babylonian Atrahasis epic, edited by Lambert and Millard (1969), tells the whole history of mankind from creation to the Flood. Tigay used this and other evidence to show how the Gilgamesh poet borrowed the Flood story. The slip is one of the clearest traces of composition in the epic.

title: 'At the mouth of the rivers' (Dilmun)
short: Enlil makes Uta-Napishtim and his wife like gods and settles them far away, 'at the mouth of the rivers'.
body: The epic does not name the place, but in the Sumerian Flood story the hero Ziusudra is placed in Dilmun, 'where the sun rises'. Dilmun is usually identified with Bahrain and the nearby Gulf coast. 'The mouth of the rivers' suggests the place where the Tigris and Euphrates reach the sea, or a mythical source of rivers. The blessing (touching their foreheads) is a ritual of divinisation.

title: The test of sleep
short: Uta-Napishtim challenges Gilgamish to stay awake six days and seven nights; he falls asleep at once.
body: If he cannot conquer sleep, the 'brother of death', how can he conquer death? The test exposes Gilgamish's human third. Uta-Napishtim's wife pities him; her husband says that humans are deceitful and will deny they slept, hence the loaves. The test is a parody of the long vigil before a divine decision: the gods, says Uta-Napishtim, cannot be assembled for Gilgamish's sake as they were for his. The failure is sudden: as soon as Gilgamish sits down, sleep 'like a mist' (Thompson: 'like a breeze') breathes over him. The scene is quietly comic as well as tragic.

title: The loaves of bread
short: Thompson understood seven stages of baking a single loaf; modern editions have seven loaves, one baked per day, each in a different state of staleness.
body: Thompson's note calls the passage difficult. George reads that the wife bakes a loaf each day and marks the wall; when Gilgamish wakes the first loaf is dried out, the second leathery, the third soggy, the fourth mouldy, and so on to the seventh still on the coals. The loaves prove how long he slept. On Thompson's reading the stages belong to one loaf, so the loaves no longer measure the days of the sleep.

title: 'A Robber hath ravished my courage'
short: Thompson's note admits 'it is not intelligible'; modern editors understand a death-demon, 'the Taker' or 'Snatcher', who has seized Gilgamish's flesh.
body: The ekkemu is a demon that seizes people. In George's version Gilgamish says that the Taker has hold of his flesh and that Death is in his bedroom: whichever way he turns, there is death. A stark moment of despair. Thompson's honesty in noting that he could not understand the line is typical of his method. Modern understanding makes it the culmination of his fear of death, which pursues him even indoors.

title: Washing and new clothes
short: Ur-Shanabi washes Gilgamish, throws his skins into the sea and dresses him in a garment that will not age until he reaches home.
body: The return to civilised appearance reverses the mourning of VIII-X and recalls Enkidu's humanisation in II. The clothes that stay fresh are a small miracle that hints at the limits of the gift: not eternal youth, just a garment that lasts a journey. The garment also symbolises the limited, practical gift that is all Uta-Napishtim can give, until his wife's intervention brings the secret of the plant.

title: The plant of rejuvenation
short: At his wife's request Uta-Napishtim reveals a thorny plant at the bottom of the sea that restores youth.
body: The plant offers not immortality but rejuvenation. It grows in the Apsu, the fresh water beneath the earth, Ea's realm. Etana sought a 'plant of birth'; Adam was barred from the tree of life (Genesis 3:22). In George's text it is a plant that restores the vital force and youth. Its location in the deep may link it with Ea and the Apsu, the source of wisdom and of the waters. It is significant that the plant is only revealed because Uta-Napishtim's wife pleads for a parting gift, a further example of women's mediation in the epic (the courtesan, Nin-sun, Siduri).

title: Diving with stones
short: Gilgamish ties heavy stones to his feet to dive for the plant: a technique used by pearl divers of the Persian Gulf.
body: Divers of Bahrain (Dilmun) traditionally weighted themselves with stones; some scholars have connected the plant with pearls or coral, which is speculative. Thompson does not comment on the technique, but the detail fits the poem's setting near the Gulf, and the plant's thorny nature has suggested coral to some readers. Such identifications remain speculative, and the text itself is concerned with the plant's power, not its biology.

title: 'Old Man Grew Young'
short: Gilgamish names the plant 'The old man has become a young man' and plans to test it on an old man of Uruk before eating it himself.
body: Thompson's hyphenated name renders the Akkadian Sibu issahir amelu (George: 'Old Man Grew Young'). His caution (testing it first) is a sign of his new prudence, or of his delay, which proves fatal. Naming the plant shows him taking possession of it, as if it were already his. The irony is that the name promises reversal of age to an 'old man', and he intends to give it first to an elder of Uruk: his first thought is for others, or for safety. The delay is fatal: he never reaches Uruk with it.

title: The journey home
short: 'At the fortieth hour ... at the sixtieth': the formula of the Cedar Forest journey (twenty and thirty leagues) returns.
body: Each league (beru) is a double-hour, so twenty leagues equals forty hours. The repetition of the formula from Tablets IV-V marks the journey back as a mirror of the journey out. The journey home with Ur-Shanabi thus repeats the shape of the journey to the Cedar Forest with Enkidu: a new companion replaces the old, and the formula marks Gilgamish's return from the edges of the world.

title: The snake steals the plant
short: While Gilgamish bathes, a snake smells the plant and takes it; in modern editions it sheds its skin as it goes.
body: George reads that the snake 'shed its slough' as it went back, an aetiology for the snake's renewal of youth by shedding its skin. Thompson has it 'uttering malison' (a curse), an older reading. Compare the serpent of Genesis 3, who also deprives man of a chance of life. The episode explains why snakes, not humans, renew themselves, and it closes the hero's last chance.

title: The 'earth-lion'
short: 'Lion of the earth' is a name for the snake: Gilgamish's labour has profited only the snake.
body: The kenning nes qaqqari, literally 'lion of the ground', is a term for a snake or reptile. Gilgamish's bitter words close the quest for life. Thompson keeps the literal translation, which preserves the oddness of the expression. The bitter recognition that he has toiled only for a snake ends the hero's quest for physical immortality and leads to his return to Uruk and its walls, the last image of the standard version.

anchor: walk on the ramparts of Erech
title: Return to the walls of Uruk
short: Gilgamish invites Ur-Shanabi to walk on the walls of Uruk and examine the bricks: the same lines as the prologue of Tablet I.
body: The ring composition is complete. In George's text the lines repeat the prologue: the walls of kiln-fired brick, laid by the Seven Sages, and the city's area of one shar city, one shar date-groves, one shar clay-pits and half a shar for Ishtar's temple. Gilgamish has failed to become immortal, but he returns to the city he built, which will endure. Many critics read this as the poem's answer to the quest.
